questions.q: What are the four actors in the equipment-checkout requirement this capstone builds?
options: Only the employee and IT, with no approval step
Admin, developer, architect, and tester
Employee, manager, IT equipment admin, and the platform itself (for overdue detection)
Employee, HR, Finance, and Legal
questions.explain: The workflow is submit (employee), approve (manager), fulfill/track (IT admin), and flag overdue items automatically (the platform).

questions.q: Per this lesson's reasoning (building on Chapter 5), why does this requirement justify its own application scope?
options: ServiceNow requires every new table to live in a custom scope
The table names are generic enough to collide with Global, and nothing outside this feature needs to touch the data directly
Scoped applications are faster to query than Global tables
There is no real reason — scope was chosen arbitrarily
questions.explain: Lesson 19/20's reasoning applies directly: generic names like "request" risk collision, and isolation is wanted since nothing else should read or write this data.

questions.q: Why should the planned request table extend task rather than start from a bare custom table?
options: Extending task is required by ServiceNow for every custom table
A bare custom table cannot have reference fields
task is the only table that supports GlideRecord queries
task already provides state, assigned_to, opened_by, and approval plumbing the workflow needs
questions.explain: Because the requirement is an approval-then-fulfillment pattern, inheriting task's existing workflow fields avoids reinventing that structure from scratch.

questions.q: In the planned fields object below, what does the comment on the equipment field indicate about the design?
options: equipment will be a free-text string field with no validation
equipment is a calculated field with no real column
equipment will be a reference field pointing to the new x_acme_eqchk_equipment lookup table
